author: reek
body: These are the last two commands the debugger design specifies and the console did not have. `Address Lookup` is here too, and it was worse than missing: it was in the menu with NO dispatch arm at all, so the key fell through to the address evaluator and answered `expr: unknown name addr`.

author: reek
body: THE ARGUMENT COUNT WAS THE INTERESTING PART. The design writes these as `dbg mem.s <addr> <bytes>` and `dbg mem.cmp <a1> <a2> <len>`, two and three arguments against a console that dispatches one line. The console's own idiom settles it: an expression moves the cursor, a command acts there, and the window is the dump length -- the rule `watch` already uses. A search is then a pattern at the cursor and a compare is the cursor against one other address. One argument each.

author: reek
body: The needle is three bytes at a known offset, and the readings are chosen so no single wrong answer satisfies them. A search that always answered "found at the cursor" would fail the offset; one that always answered "not found" would fail the hit; one that matched only the first byte would find the decoy at +16, which shares that byte and differs in the second.

author: reek
body: The compare pair is the point of the second half. The second buffer is still entirely zero, so the first difference against the first buffer is the DECOY at +16, not the needle at +64 -- the decoy is written earlier in the buffer and a compare reports the first difference, not the most interesting one. That is worth asserting exactly: an implementation that reported the last difference, or the largest, would pass a test that only demanded "they differ".
